nameStory: This elegant gull is named after Edward Sabine, a 19th-century British explorer and naturalist who studied the Arctic regions where this bird breeds. Sabine was particularly known for his work on Earth's magnetic field during polar expeditions, making him a fitting namesake for this far-northern traveler.
description: Sabine's Gull is a small, graceful seabird that's quite rare to spot in New England waters. This Arctic breeder is about the size of a dove, much smaller than the familiar Herring Gulls you see at the beach. It has a distinctive triangular wing pattern and a slightly forked tail that sets it apart from other gulls, earning it the historical nickname 'fork-tailed gull.'

idTips.label: Triangular Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Bold triangular patches of black, white, and gray create a striking geometric pattern on the wings, visible even from a distance in flight

idTips.label: Forked Tail
idTips.description: The tail has a shallow but noticeable fork or notch at the tip, unlike the square or rounded tails of most other gulls

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more delicate than common gulls, with a lighter, more buoyant flight style that seems almost tern-like

idTips.label: Dark Hood (breeding)
idTips.description: Adults in breeding plumage have a dark gray-black hood that contrasts sharply with a thin yellow bill tipped in black

idTips.label: Pelagic Behavior
idTips.description: Usually seen far from shore over open ocean waters, often following fishing boats or floating with other seabirds

habitat: In New England, Sabine's Gulls are extremely rare visitors seen only over deep ocean waters, typically miles offshore. They're most likely to be spotted from whale-watching boats or during pelagic birding trips in the Gulf of Maine. These birds prefer the open ocean environment and are almost never seen from land or in coastal harbors.

seasonality.spring: Virtually never seen in New England waters during spring migration as they follow different routes to Arctic breeding grounds.
seasonality.summer: Absent from New England as adults are busy breeding in the high Arctic tundra and feeding in northern polar waters.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for sighting occurs during fall migration (August-October) when birds may appear far offshore following storm systems.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter as most birds spend this season in warmer southern oceans off South America and Africa.

funFact: Sabine's Gulls nest in the same Arctic colonies as Arctic Terns, and the aggressive terns actually help protect the gulls' eggs and chicks from predators like Arctic foxes and jaegers — a remarkable partnership between two very different seabirds!
confusionNotes: Young Sabine's Gulls might be confused with juvenile kittiwakes, but Sabine's distinctive triangular wing pattern and forked tail are reliable field marks. Remember: 'Sabine's has the triangle design' — the bold geometric wing patches are unlike any other small gull.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Xema' comes from an old Inuit word for this bird, and some birders still use the historical name 'xeme' (pronounced 'zeem'). With only 18 recorded sightings in all of New England, seeing one is considered a major birding achievement.
compareHints: Sabine's Gull is the only member of its genus, making it unique among gulls. Compared to other small gulls like Bonaparte's Gull, Sabine's is distinguished by its triangular wing pattern, forked tail, and preference for deep ocean waters rather than harbors and shorelines. Its flight is more graceful and tern-like than the choppier wing beats of typical gulls.
